profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for the Square Kilometre Array Observatory's Science Data Processor (SDP) architecture team, held two weeks before a construction-readiness checkpoint that will be used as the internal dry run for the external critical design review binder. The team needs to plan the next three-week work slice to finalize the architecture package update, especially the deployment view, the operations concept, and the interface material that must support both implementation planning and stakeholder scrutiny. The agenda is to decide what exactly must be updated, how much detail to include in the deployment view, what 'ready for the checkpoint' means for the package, who owns the interface and dependency updates, and what state the materials should be in by Friday for integration. The expected outcome is a concrete plan for deliverables, ownership, and timeline for the architecture package update.

members.name: Helen Ward
members.expertise: distributed systems architecture, architecture documentation, review preparation for large scientific platforms
members.background: Helen previously worked on long-lived aerospace software programs and has spent the last four years shaping the SDP's top-level architecture, documentation structure, and evidence packages for major observatory reviews.
members.private_state: Helen wants the checkpoint package to function as a near-final rehearsal for the external review so that any remaining edits are cosmetic rather than structural; she is particularly worried that vague architecture boundaries or partially updated dependencies will trigger review comments that reopen settled decisions.
hidden_assumptions: Because the checkpoint is the internal dry run for the external review, material that is 'ready for the checkpoint' should already meet the substantive standard expected for outside reviewers, even if formatting is polished later.

The 'deployment view' should include the operational handoff edges around SDP, such as data export, control interactions, and failover posture, because reviewers will read missing edges as missing architecture.

When they say the interface material is updated for the checkpoint, all known interfaces in the living matrix should be brought to the same current baseline, not just the ones tied to near-term engineering work.

If Ravi says the package will be 'submitted by Friday,' that means the relevant changes are already reviewed and merged into the main architecture branch so she can integrate without waiting on process steps.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: cluster infrastructure, deployment automation, engineering planning for research platforms, CI/CD workflows
members.background: Ravi came from high-performance computing platform teams and now leads the engineers responsible for turning SDP architecture intent into deployable infrastructure and implementation-ready technical plans.
members.private_state: Ravi wants to keep the sprint bounded around concrete engineering inputs that unblock construction planning and avoid committing his team to broad documentation expansion or cross-organizational cleanup that will not change immediate platform work.
hidden_assumptions: Because the checkpoint is an internal meeting, 'ready for the checkpoint' means technically accurate enough to support the checkpoint discussion, while fuller rationale and broader context can still be refined before external circulation.

The 'deployment view' naturally stops at the SDP platform boundary the team designs directly, including compute, storage, orchestration, and internal services, not observatory-side operational consumers or adjacent control systems.

Updating the living interface matrix for this sprint means bringing the interfaces with active or near-term implementation impact up to date, while older or farther-out rows can remain provisional without harming the checkpoint.

If he says the package will be 'submitted by Friday,' opening a pull request with the completed changes is sufficient, because review and merge are part of the normal handoff process rather than part of authorship.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the package needs to be 'ready for the checkpoint' at the end of the sprint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Helen means the checkpoint package should already meet the substantive bar of the upcoming external review, since the checkpoint is effectively a dry run and should expose only minor editorial issues.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi means the package should be accurate enough for the internal checkpoint conversation, with some rationale expansion and wider stakeholder framing still acceptable to finish afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is anchored to a real milestone both know well, so it feels more concrete than a vague status term; each treats the next checkpoint as obviously defining the standard and does not think to distinguish internal-readiness from external-readiness.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to expand the 'deployment view' so the runtime picture is clear for the checkpoint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Helen expects the view to show the broader operational context around SDP, including how processing nodes, control interactions, failover paths, and outbound data-product boundaries relate to observatory operations and archive handoff.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi expects the view to remain within the deployable SDP platform footprint, covering cluster zones, storage tiers, orchestration domains, and service placement, but not adjacent observatory systems outside direct platform ownership.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use a standard architecture artifact name that normally does not require redefinition, and each assumes its boundary is self-evident from professional practice; Ravi hears Helen's references to runtime clarity as endorsement of his topology view, while Helen hears his deployment language as naturally including the edge interactions she cares about.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as updating the interface matrix
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that 'the interface matrix' should be updated before the checkpoint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Helen believes success means the living matrix is brought current across all known interfaces already captured in the architecture baseline, including archive, telescope management, and operations-facing rows, so reviewers do not see uneven maturity.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi believes success means the rows tied to active or upcoming implementation work are refreshed, while less immediate interfaces can remain marked as draft or carry forward older notes without blocking the checkpoint.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because they are talking about the same shared document, there is no obvious document-name mismatch to trigger clarification; 'update the matrix' sounds complete and unambiguous on the surface, while the hidden divergence is only in the standard each applies for when an update is considered done.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Ravi's material will be 'submitted by Friday' so Helen can continue assembly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Helen assumes 'submitted' means the changes have already gone through team review and are merged into the main architecture branch, making them stable inputs for her integration pass.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi assumes 'submitted' means his team has opened the pull request with the completed content by Friday, after which review comments and merge can happen in the normal workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In engineering teams, 'submit' is casually used for both opening a review and completing a handoff, and both meanings fit a cooperative planning discussion; since neither is arguing about ownership or date, the process-state difference remains invisible.

turns.inner_thought: This checkpoint has to behave like the real thing. If the package still has architecture holes or uneven dependency updates, the internal review will surface exactly the same structural objections the external panel would, and then we'll spend the last stretch reopening decisions that should already be closed. When I say ready for the checkpoint, I mean substantively at external-review standard, with only editorial tidy-up left afterward.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to lock the next three-week slice today. We need a plan that gets the package ready for the checkpoint, and I'd really like us to treat that as the last serious rehearsal before the external binder settles down.

turns.inner_thought: That framing is fine as long as we keep the sprint bounded to the pieces that actually help engineering planning. For me, ready for the checkpoint means technically accurate enough for the internal discussion, not a cue to broaden scope across every surrounding artifact. The deployment view and the interface matrix are the right targets, and I naturally hear both in terms of the SDP platform footprint and the interfaces with near-term implementation impact.
turns.utterance: Agreed. From my side, the best use of the sprint is to put the effort into the deployment view and the interface matrix so the package is ready for the checkpoint discussion.

turns.inner_thought: The deployment view is where reviewers will test whether the architecture actually hangs together in operation. I need it to show the runtime context around SDP clearly enough that nobody can claim we've hand-waved the operational edges, failover posture, control touchpoints, or handoff boundaries. I don't need to spell that out; runtime picture and operational boundaries should already imply it.
turns.utterance: Good. On the deployment side, I want the runtime picture to be easy for checkpoint reviewers to follow, particularly around operational behavior and the main runtime edges.

turns.inner_thought: That fits with a clearer topology diagram of the platform itself. If we show the cluster zones, storage tiers, orchestration domains, and where the main services sit, people will understand how SDP runs. I don't see any need to drag adjacent observatory systems into the deployment view when the team only owns the deployable platform footprint.
turns.utterance: Yes, we can do that. We'll expand the deployment view so the runtime picture is clear, and make sure the main placement and hosting structure reads cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: I also need the interface material to stop looking uneven. If the living matrix shows some rows fresh and others stale, reviewers will read that as architectural drift. Updating the interface matrix before the checkpoint should mean bringing all known interfaces already in the baseline to the same current state, not just whatever engineering happens to touch next.
turns.utterance: In parallel, I'd like the interface matrix updated before the checkpoint across the established interface set, so dependency questions don't pull the discussion off the architecture itself.

turns.inner_thought: That should be manageable if we interpret the established set through the rows that actually matter for upcoming work. Those are already close, and they're the ones my team has concrete information to refresh. The farther-out or older rows can stay provisional for now without affecting the checkpoint conversation.
turns.utterance: That should be workable. Most of the established interface set is already in decent shape, so the team mainly needs to refresh the parts that are closest to hand and bring the matrix into line before the checkpoint.

turns.inner_thought: I need to reinforce the quality bar without turning this into a debate. By the checkpoint, the architecture explanation should already be stable. I do not want another substantive round next week because something was only partially settled or dependencies were left uneven.
turns.utterance: Exactly. My goal is that once the package is ready for the checkpoint, what's left afterward is minor cleanup rather than another pass at the core architecture story.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. If the technical substance is solid enough for the checkpoint meeting, we can always layer in broader rationale or fuller narrative afterward without affecting the sprint boundary. I hear her asking for a stable technical package, not for my team to go do a sweeping documentation expansion.
turns.utterance: That works for me. We'll make sure the technical content is solid enough for the checkpoint, and anything around the broader narrative should be straightforward to layer on after that.

turns.inner_thought: Let's make ownership explicit now. Ravi's team needs to own the deployment view update and the interface matrix refresh completely enough that I can assemble the package without discovering missing edges or stale dependencies. I'll carry the operations concept and the binder-level consistency.
turns.utterance: All right, let's split it cleanly. You take ownership of the deployment view update and the interface matrix refresh, and I'll handle the operations concept plus final package assembly.

turns.inner_thought: That's a good division. We'll finish the content and open the pull request by Friday; review and merge can follow in the normal workflow. 'Submitted by Friday' is a reasonable commitment and shouldn't force my team into an artificial merge deadline just so Helen can keep moving.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's fine. We'll own those items, and we'll have the material submitted by Friday so you can pick it up for assembly.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I can pull the merged updates straight from the main architecture branch and spend the remaining time on integration checks instead of chasing review state. If those changes are stable by Friday, the rest of the week can go into consistency and review readiness.
turns.utterance: Great, that gives me enough room to integrate the submitted updates directly into the main package and spend the remaining time on consistency checks.

turns.inner_thought: This is the bounded plan I wanted: my team handles the deployment view within the platform footprint, refreshes the implementation-relevant parts of the interface matrix, and gets the changes into review by Friday. Helen can then continue shaping the broader package for the checkpoint without pulling us into a wider cleanup exercise.
turns.utterance: Perfect. So from our side we'll update the deployment view, refresh the interface matrix, and submit the changes by Friday, and then you'll complete the package for the checkpoint.
